steps.title: Write the ticket-price algorithm as pseudocode
steps.instructions:
A movie theatre charges by age. Here is the algorithm in plain English:

**1.** Start.

**2.** Get the customer's age.

**3.** If the age is under `13`, the ticket costs `$8`. Otherwise the ticket costs `$14`.

**4.** Print the ticket price.

**5.** End.

The chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar) shows a **different** decision, a swimming-pool lane, so you can see the shape of one: get the value, ask one question, both answers labelled, both reaching the print. It is not your answer. You design yours from the steps above.

In `README.md`, type your steps as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line** (those two lines are Start and End). Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `INPUT height` (get a value from the user)
- `IF height is 120 or more` ... `ELSE` ... `END IF` (a check with two answers, the steps inside indented)
- `SET lane TO "deep"` (start or change a value)
- `PRINT lane` (show something)

Plain English is fine. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, trace it twice by hand: once with age `9` and once with age `30`. Each should print a price.

Getting this green unlocks the 2.2.8 A2.2.1 (Part A) plan next: the same plan-before-you-write habit you will use for every graded project from here on.
hints: Get the age first: you cannot test a value you have not got yet.
ELSE is the other answer to the same question. Set one price under the IF and the other under the ELSE.
Print the price after END IF so it prints whichever answer was taken.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: Gets the age before deciding
requirements.description: Get the customer's age (input, ask, read) before the check.
requirements.hint: Add a step that gets the age before the IF.

requirements.title: The question is about 13
requirements.description: Check the age against 13 (under 13, or 13 or over).
requirements.hint: Add a check that compares the age with 13.

requirements.title: Right price for each answer
requirements.description: Under 13 costs $8 and 13 or over costs $14, on the matching branches.
requirements.hint: Under 13 gets $8 and 13 or over gets $14. Check each price is on the right branch.

requirements.title: Both answers are written
requirements.description: The decision has an ELSE (the other answer) and is closed with END IF.
requirements.hint: Write the other answer under ELSE and close the check with END IF.

requirements.title: Prints the price
requirements.hint: Add a step that prints the ticket price.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The algorithm is: get the customer's age; if the age is under 13 the ticket price is $8, otherwise $14; print the ticket price. In JavaScript: const age = Number(prompt("Age?")); let price; if (age < 13) { price = 8; } else { price = 14; } console.log(price). The point is one question about 13 with two answers carrying the right prices ($8 for under 13, $14 for 13 and over), with the age obtained before the question and the price printed. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, END FOR, CALL, PRINT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite (for example no step that gets the age, the two prices swapped, or no step that prints the price). Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
